title: Views
subtitle: CREATE VIEW — named saved queries and virtual tables
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Complex JOIN queries are written over and over again across many parts of an application. If the schema changes, every copy must be updated. Junior devs write inefficient versions; code diverges.
whyItExists.solution: A view is a named SELECT query stored in the database. Any query can SELECT from a view as if it were a table. The underlying query runs on every access.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Frequently used complex JOINs. Simplified read access for application code. Hiding sensitive columns (show view without password_hash). Abstracting schema changes.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: If the view is very expensive to compute and called often — use a materialized view (PostgreSQL) or a caching layer instead. Views in SQLite are read-only (no INSERT/UPDATE through views).

explainModes.beginner: A view is like saving a query by name. Instead of writing a 5-table JOIN every time, you save it as 'order_details' and then just SELECT * FROM order_details. The database runs the JOIN for you every time you query the view.
explainModes.simple: CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ...; — save a query. SELECT * FROM name; — query it like a table. DROP VIEW name; — remove it. CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW (PostgreSQL) — update it. Views are virtual — no data is stored. ALTER VIEW isn't supported in SQLite — drop and recreate.
explainModes.standard: Views are expanded inline at query time — the planner merges the view's SELECT with the outer query for optimization. SQLite views are always read-only. PostgreSQL: simple views over a single table without GROUP BY are sometimes updatable (INSTEAD OF triggers for complex ones). WITH CHECK OPTION prevents inserts/updates that wouldn't be visible in the view.
explainModes.technical: Materialized views (PostgreSQL): REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW name — store results physically. Fast to query (no JOIN at read time) but data is stale until refreshed. CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... WITH DATA. Concurrent refresh: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY (requires unique index). Not available in SQLite — replicate with a real table + periodic INSERT INTO ... SELECT. Views can be built on top of other views (view chaining) but deep chains can confuse the optimizer.
explainModes.deepDive: Updatable views (PostgreSQL): a view is automatically updatable if it satisfies strict conditions (single base table, no DISTINCT/GROUP BY/HAVING/LIMIT/UNION/aggregate/window function). INSTEAD OF triggers handle writes to complex views. Row-level security (PostgreSQL): combine views with RLS policies to enforce tenant isolation. CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders USING (user_id = current_setting('app.user_id')::INT). This pattern lets the application set a session variable, and the database enforces the filter on every query — zero chance of a missing WHERE clause leaking data.

content.code:
-- View: full order details (replaces repetitive 3-table join)
CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS order_details AS
SELECT
    o.id         AS order_id,
    u.name       AS customer,
    u.city,
    p.name       AS product,
    p.category,
    o.quantity,
    o.total,
    o.ordered_at
FROM orders o
JOIN users    u ON o.user_id    = u.id
JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.id;

-- Now query the view like a table
SELECT * FROM order_details;

-- Filter on the view
SELECT customer, product, total
FROM order_details
WHERE category = 'Electronics'
ORDER BY total DESC;

-- Aggregate on the view
SELECT customer, SUM(total) AS total_spent
FROM order_details
GROUP BY customer
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;

-- View: customer summary (hides the raw orders table complexity)
CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS customer_summary AS
SELECT
    u.id,
    u.name,
    u.city,
    COUNT(o.id)            AS order_count,
    COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS total_spent,
    MAX(o.ordered_at)      AS last_order_date
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.id, u.name, u.city;

SELECT * FROM customer_summary ORDER BY total_spent DESC;

-- List all views
SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'view';

-- Drop a view
-- DROP VIEW IF EXISTS order_details;

questions.question: What happens to the underlying data when you DROP VIEW?
options: The underlying tables are dropped too
Nothing — the view is just a saved SELECT; dropping it doesn't affect the tables
All rows returned by the view are deleted
The view is archived, not deleted
questions.explanation: A view stores no data of its own — it's just a named query. DROP VIEW removes the saved query definition. The underlying tables and their data are completely unaffected. To delete data, you'd use DELETE FROM on the actual tables.

faq.q: Are views faster than writing the same query directly?
faq.a: Not inherently — a view is expanded inline at query time, so the database runs the same JOIN. However, views encourage writing the query once correctly (with proper indexes), and then it's reused everywhere. For performance, PostgreSQL's materialized views store the result physically and are much faster to read — at the cost of potentially stale data until refreshed.

examples: CREATE VIEW public_users AS SELECT id, name, city FROM users — hide email/password
CREATE VIEW sales_report AS SELECT ... complex join ... — expose to non-SQL analysts
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_stats AS SELECT ... REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY daily_stats — nightly dashboard refresh
